messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Robert was fifty-six, a pianist who had spent thirty years in recording studios and small venues, known for his steady hands and his ability to read a room. That steadiness ended two years ago, one night after a session, when a colleague he trusted followed him to his car. The man wore a heavy cologne—something woody, sweet—and when Robert refused his advances, the violence came fast: a blow to the face that split his lip, then a hand clamped over his mouth, blood smearing across his own cheek, the scent of the cologne flooding his nose as the assault unfolded. He remembered that smell with unbearable clarity. He remembered the blood on his tongue. But other parts—how he got home, what he said to his wife, the hours that followed—were blank, as if someone had erased them. He could not tell a coherent story of what happened, even to himself.

In the months afterward, Robert found that whenever a memory fragment began to surface—the weight of a hand, the metallic taste—he would mentally shove it away before it could fully take shape. That pushing had become automatic: a way to survive. He never allowed himself to feel or express anger about what had been done to him, because anger felt like a door to something he could not control. And he began avoiding people in authority—police officers, uniformed security guards—because they made him feel small and powerless all over again. He also stopped seeing the friends he had socialised with before the assault; their faces belonged to a time he could no longer inhabit, and their casual questions about his quietness felt like accusations.

The world outside his home grew dangerous. Robert only felt safe in a very limited number of places: his studio, the room where he practiced, the corner of the couch where he could see both doors. Any sudden movement by his wife or a passerby put him immediately on guard. His irritability spiked; he snapped at his wife for walking up behind him, for touching his shoulder without warning. When he caught a whiff of a sweet, woody cologne in a grocery store, his entire body locked into high alert—a racing pulse, a clammy chill—and he left the cart abandoned. The same happened when he saw blood, even a paper cut, or violence on a screen. His hypervigilance made him scan every scent, every gesture, every hint of force; the more he scanned, the more triggers he found. And the very act of trying to recall the assault caused him to become acutely aware of potential threats around him, as if the memory sharpened his danger radar.

A cycle had tightened over the months. A sudden movement from his wife triggered a flash of the assault—the hand, the weight—and that flash left him feeling exposed, which in turn made him more vigilant, more irritable, more likely to notice a cologne or a raised voice. His avoidance of authority figures and old social contacts narrowed his life, but it also primed him: every rare encounter with a former friend or a security guard became a powerful trigger, because his system had been sensitized by isolation. And by deliberately suppressing his anger and dodging anything that might remind him of that night, he kept his memory fragmented; the story never cohered, the blank spaces never filled, and the partial clarity of the bloody moments remained frozen.

Eventually, Robert stopped accepting gigs that required him to enter unfamiliar venues. His income shrank, and his wife began sleeping in the guest room after he woke her one night screaming, unable to say what he had seen. It was she who finally urged him to call a therapist. He came to the first session with his hands clenched on his knees, afraid that if he let the memories finish forming, he would fall apart completely. But he was also afraid of staying where he was—afraid that the safe zone would keep shrinking until there was nothing left of the musician he used to be.

violation_explanations: No paragraph conveys that the memory causes or amplifies triggers; triggers are externally driven and not shown as resulting from the memory.
No paragraph conveys that a sense of threat leads to the memory; instead, triggers lead to memory and memory leads to threat.
